extracted.intended_audience: scholars, translators, and students of Archimedes/classical Greek mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and documenting the conventional Greek mathematical terminology, syntactic constructions, and proof-writing idioms used by Archimedes (as explained in the Introduction). Useful for translators, editors, and historians of ancient mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Passive 'let ... be conceived' construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of passive infinitival/imperative constructions to express 'let ... be conceived/let ... be drawn' (e.g. "Let straight lines be conceived to be drawn νοείσθωσαν", "let the sphere be conceived to be cut νοείσθω ἡ σφαῖρα τετμημένη").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Passive participles and imperatives are standard for setting up imagined constructions (e.g. "ἐγγραφὲν σχῆμα" for an inscribed figure). Sometimes the participle for 'drawn' is omitted (example: ἀπ᾽ αὐτοῦ νοείσθω ἐπιφάνεια). Use these forms when describing ideal or supposed constructions in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active constructions and alternatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Active voice occurs but less often; constructions include (1) ἐὰν with subjunctive (e.g. ἐὰν τέμωμεν 'if we cut'), (2) participles indicating possibility (e.g. δυνατόν ἐστιν ἐγγράφοντα...), and (3) first person singular narrative (e.g. λαμβάνω δύο εὐθείας 'I take two straight lines').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that Archimedes sometimes uses active forms to narrate operations or processes; examples given show modality and staged descriptions (possibility, iterative constructions). When translating, preserve the nuance (subjunctive vs participle vs indicative first person).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genitive absolute of passive participle
rubrics_metrics.description: The genitive of the passive participle is used absolutely to set background suppositions (examples: εὑρεθέντος δή 'it being supposed found', ἐγγραφέντος δή '(the figure) being inscribed').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate as circumstantial clauses ('it being supposed/found that...') and preserve the absolute construction's backgrounding function in proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vocabulary for constructing similarity/equality/operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Special verbs/phrases for actions: 'to make a figure similar' δμοιώσαι, 'to find experimentally' ὀργανικῶς λαβεῖν, 'to cut into unequal parts' εἰς ἄνισα τέμνειν.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these conventional verbs when describing geometric operations; they carry conventional meanings in the context of propositions and constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addition: verbs and expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: To add: προστίθημι; passive notion often with πρόσκειμαι. Phrases for adding usually followed by πρός (with acc.) or sometimes dative. 'Being added together' συντίθεσθαι; sums expressed by συναμφότερος and related forms. Words for 'together with' include μετὰ, σύν, τε, καί; participle of προσλαμβάνω also used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When translating additive statements, attend to the choice between πρός and dative (to which the addition was made), and to special nouns/adjectives for 'sum' (συναμφότερος, τὸ συναμφότερον). Examples in the text illustrate idiomatic ordering and agreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subtraction and difference vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: To subtract from: ἀφαιρεῖν ἀπό; passive/participle forms for 'taken away' ἀφῃρημένος; 'remainder' is λοιπός; 'difference' or 'excess' ὑπεροχή (and verb ὑπερέχειν); opposite expressed by λείπεται (with gen.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate remainders and excesses with these terms; examples show algebraic equivalences and constructions ('the remainder is denoted by λοιπός'). The text supplies sample phrasings for algebraic-like statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication vocabulary and constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: To multiply: πολλαπλασιάζω; to multiply by (use dative) πεπολλαπλασιάσθω ὁ A τῷ ©; 'multiplied into' sometimes ἐπί (with acc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve case usage (dative for multiplicand) and the occasional use of ἐπί to indicate multiplicative result, as shown in examples (rectangles, solids).

rubrics_metrics.name: Division vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: To divide: διαιρεῖν; imperative/infinitive forms used for 'let it be divided' (διῃρήσθω εἰς τρία ἴσα...) ; 'to be divisible by' μετρεῖσθαι ὑπό.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translate quantified division and divisibility statements using these verbs and note constructions marking the points of division.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion and ratio terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: Ratio: λόγος; proportional: ἀνάλογον; proportion: ἀναλογία. Archimedes sometimes uses λέγω in ways that illuminate Euclid's ratio definition. Mean proportional: μέση ἀνάλογον; two mean proportionals: δύο μέσαι ἀνάλογον; fourth proportional: τετάρτα ἀνάλογον.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these technical terms for ratios and proportions; recognize expressions for continued proportion (κατὰ τὸ συνεχές) and the way Archimedes refers to ratios in relation to other magnitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expressions for 'same ratio' and comparative ratios
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases for 'have the same ratio' (e.g. τὸν αὐτὸν ἔχοντι λόγον), 'to have a less (or greater) ratio' ἔχειν λόγον ἐλάσσονα (or μείζονα) with genitive of the second term; examples of duplicate/triplicate ratios (διπλασίονα, τριπλασίονα, ἡμιόλιος for sesquialterate).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When rendering comparative ratio statements, keep the comparative constructions and special multiplicative ratio adjectives; distinguish between 'duplicate' (as used) and 'double' in modern parlance (text warns of contrasts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compound ratios and ratio transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Compound ratio: λόγος συνημμένος/συγκείμενος; technical transformations: ἐναλλάξ (alternando/permute), ἀνάπαλιν (invertendo), σύνθεσις λόγου (componendo), διαίρεσις λόγου (diwidendo/dividendo—note textual caveat), ἀναστροφὴ λόγου (conversion), διέ ἴσου (ex aequali).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the standard names for algebraic-style manipulations of proportions. The text gives their meanings (e.g., συνθέντι = componendo a+b:b = c+d:d) and warns about possibly misleading translations (e.g., 'diwidendo'). Use the Greek technical terms with the supplied meanings in exegesis or translation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetical multiples and expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiples are expressed as διπλάσιος, τριπλάσιος, τετραπλασία etc.; general 'multiple' πολλαπλάσιος; adverbial forms twice/three times: δὶς, τρίς; phrases for 'as many times as' (ὁσάκις συγκείται ... τοσαυτάκις συγκείσθω...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preserve idiomatic adverbials and adjectival agreement with the magnitude's gender. Examples show compounded phrases (e.g. 'five times the sum of AB, BE' rendered in Greek).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naming of submultiples and fractions
rubrics_metrics.description: Submultiples: ordinal+μέρος (e.g. ἕβδομον μέρος for one-seventh); one-half is ἥμισυς. Non-unity numerator expressed by ordinal plus compound substantive (e.g. δύο τριταμόρια for two-thirds). Special names for mixed/ improper fractions: ἡμιόλιος (one-and-a-half), ἐπίτριτος (one-and-a-third); mixed numbers given as integer then fraction with καὶ ἔτι or καί.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow Greek naming conventions when reconstructing or translating fractional statements; the text gives patterns for denominators when large numbers require circumlocution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrases for approximation/inequalities (circumference/diameter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Example phrasings for saying circumference is less than 31 1/7 times diameter but greater than 31 1/7 times minus a part: elaborate compound constructions given (e.g. παντὸς κύκλου ἡ περίμετρος τῆς διαμέτρου τριπλασίων ἐστί, καὶ ἔτι ὑπερέχει ἐλάσσονι μὲν ἢ ἑβδόμῳ μέρει...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the multi-clause Greek formulas for bounding statements; the Introduction highlights typical idioms for expressing 'less than' and 'greater than' with fractional parts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure/commensurability vocabulary
rubrics_metrics.description: To measure: μετρεῖν; common measure: κοινὸν μέτρον; commensurable: σύμμετρος; incommensurable: ἀσύμμετρος.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These technical terms are standard for Discourses on commensurability and require consistent rendering in translation/commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanics terminology and phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Mechanics: τὰ μηχανικά; weight: βάρος; centre of gravity: κέντρον τοῦ Bapeος; lever: ζυγός or ζύγιον; horizon: ὃ δρίζων; suspension verbs and equilibrium phrases (e.g. κρεμάσθω, ἰσορροπεῖν, ἰσορρεπής).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the canonical technical words in Archimedes' mechanical arguments; note case patterns (e.g. κέντρον with genitive of the body) and idiomatic locutions for 'in equilibrium' and 'to incline'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology for theorems, problems, and requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorem: θεώρημα; problem: πρόβλημα; expressions for 'proposed/propounded' τὰ προβεβλημένα; 'requirement' or direction: ἐπίταγμα; use of πρόκειμαι in place of a passive 'it was proposed' (ὅπερ προέκειτο εὑρεῖν).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When identifying parts of propositions, use these nouns to mark theorem vs problem and to render the statement of what is to be demonstrated or constructed. ἐπίταγμα denotes both construction requirements and requirements on the solver.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis and synthesis in problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Analysis: ἀνάλυσις; Synthesis: σύνθεσις. The synthesis is often introduced with συντεθήσεται τὸ πρόβλημα οὕτως; analysis and synthesis of problems are sometimes presented separately and referenced in closing remarks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the classical structure: analysts introduce the method (analysis) and then give the constructive proof (synthesis); translators should keep these labels to make the method visible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination (διορισμός) of limits for problems
rubrics_metrics.description: διορισμός indicates the determination of the limits within which a solution is possible; if a solution is always possible, the problem 'does not involve a διορισμός' (οὐκ ἔχει διορισμόν), otherwise it 'has a διορισμόν'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this technical term when discussing existence/parameter restrictions of geometric constructions; it signals that a problem includes specification of admissible ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phrasing for data and hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Given' uses parts of δίδωμι (δοθείς, δεδομένος, διδόμενος): e.g. δεδόσθω κύκλος 'let a circle be given'. 'Given in position' θέσει. Hypotheses: ὑποτίθεμαι, passive ὑπόκειμαι; constructions: ὑποκείσθω τὰ εἰρημένα. Quoting hypotheses in reductio uses past tense of ὑπόκειμαι with varied constructions: (1) adjective/participle, (2) infinitive, (3) passive plane supposed drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Render given data and suppositions using the appropriate participial forms; note the special conventions when reintroducing a hypothesis in later steps (past tense and three syntactic patterns).

rubrics_metrics.name: Idiomatic logical connectors and their uses
rubrics_metrics.description: Conjunctions/inferential words: therefore ἀρα; οὖν and τοίνυν used to mark the starting-point of an argument (weaker than 'therefore'); since ἐπεί; because διότι. διά + accusative expresses reason ('because'), διά + genitive expresses means ('by means of').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the subtle differences in strength/role among ἀρα, οὖν, τοίνυν when translating arguments; use διά with the appropriate case to reflect reason vs means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adaptation of proofs to similar cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases indicating 'the proof is the same' use constructions like ὁμοίως, ἀπόδειξις ἅπερ, μεταγαγεῖν τὸν ὅμοιον λόγον, and indicate when replacing a diameter by another will 'make no difference' (δὲ οὐδέν, εἴτε... εἴτε...).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These idioms mark transfer of an argument from one geometrical setting to an analogous one; preserve the wording to show the intended generality of the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Concluding and impossibility phrases
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard conclusions: δῆλον οὖν ἐστι ('the proposition is therefore obvious'), δέδεικται, φανερὸν οὖν ἐστιν, ὃ ἔδει δείξαι. For absurdity/impossibility: ὅπερ ἄτοπον, οὐκ ἀδύνατον. Example of rhetorical double negatives given.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep these canonical closing formulas to mark the end of demonstrations or reductio steps; they are standard markers in classical proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direction and concavity vocabulary and case patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases for 'in the same direction' ἐπὶ τὰ αὐτά (with dative), 'in the other direction' ἐπὶ τὰ ἕτερα; 'concave in the same direction' ἐπὶ τὰ αὐτά κοίλη; 'on each side of' ἐφ᾽ ἑκάτερα (with gen.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the specified case government for spatial/directional idioms; examples show when genitive vs dative vs prepositional forms are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Greek use of definite article where English uses 'any'
rubrics_metrics.description: Greek often uses 'the given/the every' (e.g. πᾶσα πυραμὶς τρίτον μέρος ἐστὶ τοῦ πρίσματος) instead of English 'any'; Greeks say 'every circle', 'every straight line' rather than 'any circle'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reflect this article usage in translation choices and explanatory notes; it affects quantificational reading (universal rather than indefinite).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terminology for arithmetic and geometric progressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Arithmetic progression phrasing: magnitudes 'exceed each other by an equal' (ὑπερέχοντα); common difference ὑπεροχά; least τὸ ἐλάχιστον; greatest τὸ μέγιστον. Geometrical progression: ἀνάλογον, series ἀναλογία, term τὶς τῶν ἐν τᾷ αὐτᾷ ἀναλογίᾳ; 'numbers in geometrical progression beginning from unity' ἀριθμοὶ ἀνάλογον ἀπὸ μονάδος.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these technical nouns when discussing sequences and series; note phrasing for locating terms by distance from unity (example construction given).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foundational assumptions (axioms) used in proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Archimedes' premised assumptions: (1) of lines with same extremities the straight line is least; (2) for concave lines included between others the included is lesser; (3) of surfaces with same extremities the plane is least; (4) similar inclusion rule for surfaces; (5) of unequal magnitudes the greater exceeds the less by a magnitude which, when added to itself, can be made to exceed any assigned comparable magnitude.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these statements as the operative axioms/assumptions for subsequent propositions; translators and commentators should present them as the basic premises used throughout the book (they are more definitional than modern axioms in prose form).
